title: A Hill Is Held

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Ninth Saying: Where the land has no shape, you will be asked what shape it should have.*

The hill did not stand so much as it wandered. It was a tall, slate-grey rise on the eastern horizon, its peak shifting imperceptibly as the afternoon light shifted with it. To the untrained eye, it was a static object. To Isla, who had spent the last three hours staring at it through the sightglass, it was a slow-motion drift.

"It moved," she said, tapping the field-book. "Four paces. Since dawn."

Mags looked up from the pot where a stew was bubbling with aggressive enthusiasm. "Hills do not move, Isla. They are rocks. Rocks are patient."

"This one is not patient. It is loose." Isla pointed with her pencil. "Look at the base. The shadow line is not straight. It is wandering."

Vasht stood at the edge of their camp, his hat brim tilted against the sun. He did not look surprised. He looked tired, in the way of a man who has been waiting for a specific problem to arrive so he can finally solve it. "It is a feature of the Unmade," he said laconically. "The land here has no anchor. It drifts with the tides of its own inertia. We cannot triangulate from a moving point. If we fix our station here, and the hill moves, our angles are wrong. Our distances are wrong. The whole figure collapses."

"So we fix it?" Joss asked. He was sharpening a chisel on a stone, the sound rhythmic and sharp.

"We must fix it," Vasht said. "Before we move on. It is the first true obstacle. The first choice."

Isla felt a cold prickle at the base of her neck. A choice. In the Guild, they had measured existing things. They had verified the work of others. Here, on the edge of the blank sheet, there was no existing thing. There was only the potential for a hill.

"How do you fix a hill?" Mags asked, stirring the stew with a wooden spoon.

"By giving it a shape," Vasht said. "And by holding that shape in truth."

Isla looked at the drifting peak. It was tall, lonely, and uncertain. It looked like a question that had been left unanswered for a very long time. She picked up her compass and checked the declination again, just to be sure the world was still where she thought it was.
pages.image: A vast, pale salt flat under a wide sky, with a single tall, slate-grey hill on the distant horizon appearing slightly blurred or shifting; in the foreground, a small camp with a wagon and tents, and Isla in a mustard-yellow coat pointing at the hill with a brass compass.

pages.text:
The survey of a loose hill was less a measurement of a static object than a tracking of a slow, restless process. Isla set the level on its tripod, the brass legs biting into the crystalline ground with a satisfying click. She held the staff steady, her hand as unshaking as a plumb line, while Mags read the backsight from the staff beside her.

"Five-foot-two," Mags called out, her voice clear and crisp in the dry air.

Isla turned the telescope, focusing the crosshairs on the staff held by Joss on the slope above. "Foresight?"

"Three-foot-eight."

Isla wrote the numbers down in the field-book, the ink spreading slightly on the cheap paper. The difference between the two readings was the height difference, a simple arithmetic fact that connected one point to another. But a hill is not merely two points; it is a continuous surface that demands a map of its rise and fall. She moved the level to a new position, establishing a fresh benchmark, and repeated the sequence: backsight, foresight, record, move.

"Contour lines," Vasht said, standing behind her with his hat brim tilted against the sun. "Lines of equal height. Connect the dots. What is the slope like?"

Isla looked at her field-book, the columns of numbers arranging themselves into a pattern. On the south side, the gradient was gentle, a long, easy rise that suggested a smooth, walkable path. On the north side, the numbers jumped sharply, indicating a steep, abrupt change in elevation. A cliff. A sheer drop.

"It’s a shelf," Isla said, tracing the digits with a finger. "A long, flat shelf on the south, and a wall on the north."

"Is that true?" Vasht asked. "Or is that just what the loose land is doing right now?"

Isla frowned, checking her arithmetic for the third time. The numbers were consistent. The triangle held. The math was true. But the land was still drifting, and the cliff was not a fixed cliff but a potential one, waiting to be defined.

"Then we decide," Isla said. "We choose the shape."

Vasht nodded slowly, his eyes softening with a rare smile. "You do. I am only the teacher. The hand must be yours."

Isla looked at the jagged, unstable face of the hill. It was ugly and unformed, likely to slide if it rained, blocking the view with its roughness. It was a bad hill. But it was the only hill there was. She thought of the ferry-chains her father forged, where every link had to be tested and every link had to hold. A hill was just a chain of earth, and she had to decide how strong it was.
pages.image: Isla in her mustard-yellow coat kneeling on the salt flat, reading a brass level instrument with a staff held by Joss in a rust-red shirt and leather apron; Mags in a teal jacket stands nearby holding the staff steady, with a tall, grey, jagged hill rising behind them.

pages.text:
The field-book lay open on the plane-table, its corners fluttering against the wind with the restless energy of trapped birds. Isla held her pencil, the brass nib hovering a fraction of an inch above the paper. The south slope was easy to render; she drew it as a smooth, gentle curve, an inviting line that promised nothing but easy walking. The north side, however, was the problem that demanded a decision.

If she drew a cliff, she was admitting the land was unstable, fixing a flaw into the permanent record. If she drew a slope, she was creating a feature that did not yet exist, inventing a path where there was only air. But a hill requires a north side. It requires a shape.

She looked out at the horizon, where the Pale stretched white and empty beyond the ridge. If she made the north side a cliff, it would become a barrier, a wall that closed the country off. If she made it a slope, it would become a way through, a passage that invited the world in.

"There is no shape," Vasht said quietly, his voice low enough that the wind almost took it. He had been watching her for a long time, his grey eyes steady. "The ink will only hold what you draw. If you draw nothing, it remains loose. If you draw a cliff, it becomes a cliff. If you draw a slope, it becomes a slope."

Isla thought of the farmers in the Marches, who needed water for their cattle. The hill was high, and the land below was dry. If she made the north side a slope, she could place a spring at its foot, a source that would feed the valley rather than block it.

"It would be a choice," she said, her voice tight. "Not a measurement."

"It is always a choice," Vasht replied. "That is what the Catechism means. You are not describing the world. You are deciding it."

Isla’s hand trembled, just slightly, a tremor she had to fight down with the steady pressure of her wrist. She thought of her father’s chains, how strength came from tension, from knowing exactly where the load fell. She did not want a wall. She wanted a home.

She drew the north slope. Gentle. A rise of thirty feet. And at the base, where the line curved back into the earth, she drew a small, dark mark. A spring.

Vasht watched the ink dry, his face neutral, devoid of judgment. He looked at the paper, then at the hill, and finally back at her.

"Are you sure?" he asked.

"Yes," Isla said, setting the pencil down. "It is better."
pages.image: Close-up of Isla’s hand holding a brass pencil over a field-book on a wooden plane-table, drawing a curved line on paper; in the background, the blurred shape of the grey hill and the white salt flat, with the wind blowing her auburn hair.

pages.text:
The sealing was a ritual of quiet precision. Isla applied the guild ink, watching the black liquid settle into the paper's grain with the heavy patience of a poured foundation. She traced the lines of the sheet, her hand moving with the steady, practiced grace that had earned her her place in the Guild. The ink dried, and the paper settled.

Then, the hill breathed.

It was not a sound of thunder or crash. It was a long, deep exhalation, a ripple of light that spread from the base of the hill outwards, touching the salt flat and fading into the distance. The jagged cliff on the north side smoothed out, the rock grinding and shifting with a low hum, like a giant settling into a chair.

Isla watched, her pulse steady in her throat. The cliff was gone, replaced by a gentle slope that was green and soft. And at the foot of the hill, a thin silver line appeared. Water.

Mags ran to the spring first. She knelt down, cupped her hands, and drank, then opened her eyes to look at Isla with a wide, delighted grin.

"Sweet," Mags said. "Like a secret."

Joss laughed, a bright, startled sound. "It’s water, Mags. It’s just water."

"No, it isn’t," Mags said, shaking her head. "It’s fresh. It’s cold. It’s perfect."

Isla walked to the foot of the hill and placed her hand on the grass, which was real, which was there, which she had made. The fear that had been coiling in her stomach for the last hour unspooled, replaced by a warm, heavy satisfaction. She looked at Joss, who was watching her with an expression she did not quite know how to read. It was not admiration, but something softer, something like respect.

"Well done," he said.

She nodded, unable to speak. The hill was held, the land was fixed, and for the first time, Isla felt that she was not just measuring the world but building it.
pages.image: The grey hill now transformed into a gentle green slope, with a thin silver stream flowing from its base onto the white salt flat; Mags in a teal jacket kneeling by the water drinking, while Isla in her mustard coat stands with her hand on the grass, looking pleased.

pages.text:
That night, the camp settled into a quiet that felt different from the silence of the Guild, less like a held breath and more like the rest after a long day’s work. The stars above were sharp and bright, scattered across the dark sky like a handful of silver filings dropped from a workshop bench. Isla sat at the field desk, the lantern casting a warm, yellow pool of light on her notes, while Vasht sat in his chair, his hat removed, his grey eyes tired but alert.

"You should be proud," he said, his voice low. "But you should also be afraid."

Isla looked up, her pencil hovering over the paper. "Why?"

"Because it is true," Vasht said, leaning forward slightly. "The hill is fixed. The spring is real. People will live there. They will drink that water. They will graze their cattle on that slope. You have made a promise, Isla. A promise to the land, and to those who will come after you."

He paused, letting the silence fill the space between the tent poles and the stars.

"Never draw anything you are not willing to live under. Because you will have to live with it. Every line you draw is a choice. And every choice has a consequence."

Isla stared at him, the words settling into her mind with the same careful precision she applied to a traverse. She looked down at her field-book, at the neat lines of the hill she had drawn. They looked different now, not just as a record of angles and distances, but as a responsibility that would outlast her.

She picked up her pencil and, in the margin of the page, wrote a single line. *Accuracy is a form of care.* She underlined it twice, the graphite pressing firmly into the paper.

Vasht watched her, and for the first time that evening, he smiled. It was a small, faint curve of the mouth, but it reached his eyes, softening the lines around them.

"Good," he said. "Now sleep. We have a long way to go."

Isla closed the book and leaned back in her chair, the leather creaking softly under her weight. The stars wheeled overhead, indifferent and vast, but she felt different. She felt grounded, as if her boots had sunk into firm earth rather than loose sand. And for the first time, she was not afraid of the blank sheet. She was ready to fill it.
pages.image: Night scene at the camp, with a single lantern glowing on a field desk; Isla in her mustard coat sitting at the desk writing in a book, while Master Vasht in his grey coat and felt hat sits in a wooden chair nearby, watching her with a gentle expression, under a starry sky.
